expected.longDescription: Marathon 2: Durandal remastered on the open-source Aleph One engine, with modern widescreen resolutions, 60 fps mouselook and cross-platform support. The XBLA HD assets provide updated graphics, and the original story and levels are unchanged.

set.longDescription:
Marathon 2: Durandal is the middle of Bungie's great pre-Halo trilogy, and many people consider it the best of the three. Set seventeen years after the first game, it has you woken from stasis by Durandal, a rampant AI with his own agenda, and sent to search the ruins of Lh'owon, homeworld of the S'pht. PlayBound runs it on Aleph One, the open-source continuation of Bungie's own engine, on Windows, macOS and Linux.

The shooting is good, but what still sets it apart is how it tells its story. Terminals are scattered through each level, and reading them is how the plot moves forward: long, witty, often unsettling text from an artificial intelligence who is enjoying himself far too much. It was a great deal more ambitious than anything else in the genre at the time, and it is still rewarding to read now.

Graphics have been updated from the Xbox Live Arcade remake, and the single-player campaign is the main reason to come. Up to eight people can also join in co-op or multiplayer through a global lobby. Fans have added dozens of community scenarios to it too. Bungie allowed the trilogy to be freely redistributed, so it costs nothing. Start here if you only want to try one.

expected.longDescription: Where the story began: defend the colony ship UESC Marathon against the Pfhor. Includes the complete original 1994 scenario running on Aleph One with high-resolution assets.

set.longDescription:
Marathon is where Bungie's reputation for telling stories inside shooters began. Released in 1994, this first game has you aboard a colony ship under attack by the alien Pfhor, in a desperate fight for survival, with the ship's damaged AIs as your only source of guidance and information. It runs here on Aleph One, the open-source engine continued from Bungie's own, with builds for Windows, macOS and Linux.

The core is simple: find your way through the ship, shoot the aliens and read the terminals. Those terminals are the sole source of story, and that is what made it stand out in a year full of Doom's imitators. What begins as simple mission orders gradually becomes something much stranger, as you start to doubt who is actually telling you what to do, and why.

As the oldest of the trilogy, it feels it. Levels can be mazy and the combat is less refined than in its sequels, and modern players may find the controls and map design a real test of patience. It rewards those who take their time and read everything, though, and its story sets up Durandal and Infinity. Bungie allowed the trilogy to be freely redistributed, so all it asks of you is the time. Play it first if you want the story in order.

expected.longDescription: Marathon Infinity concludes the trilogy with non-linear realities, multiple timelines and expanded multiplayer weapons, on the Aleph One engine.

set.longDescription:
Marathon Infinity is the strangest and most ambitious game in Bungie's trilogy, and it is not the one to start with. It runs on the same engine as Durandal, here through the open-source Aleph One, but it pushes you through at least three alternate timelines, including one where you are never captured by Durandal and another where you have to destroy him. The story is deliberately dreamlike and fractured, and fans have been arguing about what it means for decades.

If you have played the first two, that is the attraction. Terminals still carry the plot, yet now they question what you think you know, and levels fold back on versions of events that may never have happened. It is hard, it is confusing, and it will not explain itself, which suits a game that ends in such an unusual place.

It also has a second life. Infinity is the version most online Marathon matches use, thanks to its maps, so it is also where you should go for multiplayer, with up to eight players in a global lobby. Modders have long used it as a base, and the engine supports dozens of community-made games. Play Marathon and Durandal first for the story, or jump straight here with friends for the deathmatch. Like the others in the series, it is free.

expected.longDescription: The original 1994 Tamriel RPG released free by Bethesda, packaged to run with DOSBox emulation and authentic MT-32 style audio.

set.longDescription:
The Elder Scrolls: Arena is where it all began. Bethesda's 1994 DOS game was the first in the series that later produced Morrowind and Skyrim, and although it looks and plays very differently, the ambition is already clear. You are imprisoned by a usurper, set free by a vision of a dead friend, and sent out across all of Tamriel to reassemble the Staff of Chaos, in a world with far more towns and dungeons than anyone could need.

The scale is what still impresses. The whole continent is here, an estimated 160,000 square kilometres by one reckoning, generated largely by algorithm rather than built by hand. That also explains its limits: many places repeat, the wilderness has little in it, and the main quest is a long series of dungeons. It is hard and often unforgiving, particularly in the first hour, and new characters die quickly.

Today, it is best approached as history, or by the sort of player who likes old RPGs on their own terms. Bethesda made it free in 2004, and it runs on modern PCs through DOSBox, which PlayBound takes care of. If you want a friendlier version of the same idea, then Daggerfall is the next step. For a modern engine in progress, try the OpenTESArena edition.

expected.longDescription: The unaltered 1996 MS-DOS release of Daggerfall, run through DOSBox for historical accuracy.

set.longDescription:
This is the original 1996 release of The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall, exactly as Bethesda shipped it, and it remains one of the most ambitious role-playing games ever made. Its world was claimed to be the size of Great Britain, with an actual map estimated at around 161,600 square kilometres, covering 44 kingdoms across nine climate regions and more than 15,000 towns, villages and dungeons. Much of that was generated by algorithm, which explains both how it exists at all and why many places feel alike.

Its systems go further than the later games in the series would dare. You design your own class with custom skills and flaws, join guilds, buy houses and ships, take out loans from banks and deal with politics between factions. Its dungeons are huge three-dimensional mazes that have defeated plenty of players, so expect to get lost.

You should know the trade-offs of this version. It is the unaltered DOS game, played through DOSBox, so it has period controls and period bugs. That makes it the right choice for historians and purists. Most new players will have a far better time with the Daggerfall Unity edition, which uses the same data on a modern engine. Bethesda made the game free in 2009, so trying it costs nothing.

expected.longDescription: The original 2002 32-bit Morrowind executable, for players who want to use older mods that depend on it.

set.longDescription:
This is Morrowind as Bethesda released it: the Game of the Year Edition of the 2002 RPG, with both of its expansions and the original engine. It is the game many people still point to when they say open-world RPGs used to be stranger. You arrive on the alien island of Vvardenfell as a prisoner with a mysterious past, and the game then more or less leaves you to it, with no quest markers and directions given in the form of actual directions.

That world is the reason to play. Giant silt striders carry you across ash wastes, mushroom-shaped towns grow from the land, and the politics of the Dunmer houses are as dense as the many in-game books describing them. Tribunal adds the capital city of Mournhold in a story that is, by Morrowind's standards, almost linear. Bloodmoon goes the other way, an open-ended trip to the frozen island of Solstheim, where you can become a werewolf.

The honest catch is that the original engine shows its age, with early combat that relies on dice rolls you cannot see. For most new players, the OpenMW edition is a smoother way to play with the same data, but this one is right for anybody who wants the 2002 experience. You need your own copy.

expected.longDescription: The official launcher managed by Jagex. Supports Jagex accounts, automatic updates and official client launches.

set.longDescription:
Old School RuneScape is a piece of 2007 preserved by popular demand. After a player poll in 2013, Jagex brought back an old version of its browser-era MMO, and it has kept growing since, with players voting on changes. This edition uses the official Jagex Launcher, which is the standard way to get in on desktop. RuneLite, listed separately, is the popular open-source alternative client.

Its pleasures are slow ones. You raise skills by doing them, chopping trees and cooking fish as much as fighting, and those long, quiet grinds are exactly what many people come for. Quests are often the highlight, as they tend to be funnier and better written than you might expect from a game of this age, and there are plenty of hard bosses for later on.

It is free to start. Free accounts get 15 skills and 20 quests, with access to Asgarnia, Misthalin and most of the Wilderness, which is plenty of game. Membership adds far more map, more skills, many more quests and most of the minigames, and you can even buy it with in-game gold through membership bonds. It is an easy game to keep in the background while you do something else, which might be why people have been playing it for so long.

This is Old School RuneScape through Steam, the same game on the same servers as the official client, with Steam handling the install and tracking your hours. Choose it if you keep your library in Steam or want an easy way to show friends what you are up to. If you want the extra plugins and overlays, RuneLite is listed as its own edition.

The game is Jagex's 2007-era MMO, brought back after a 2013 player poll and developed since then with its community voting on changes. You train skills by doing them, from woodcutting and fishing to combat, and work through quests that are often funnier and more inventive than you would expect. It has a calm, repetitive rhythm that many people use to wind down, and very demanding bosses for those who want a challenge.

The free tier is generous, with 15 skills, 20 quests and access to Asgarnia, Misthalin and most of the Wilderness. Membership adds over three times as much map, additional skills and most minigames, and it can be bought with in-game gold through membership bonds if you stick around long enough. Nothing here needs a powerful PC. PlayBound opens the Steam page, which takes care of the install, so you can be chopping your first tree in minutes.

expected.longDescription: SWG Infinity is a long-running Star Wars Galaxies emulator. Download clients and launchers only from Infinity's official site; PlayBound helps set up the connection.

set.longDescription:
SWG Infinity brings back Star Wars Galaxies as many people remember it best: before the Combat Upgrade and the New Game Enhancements changed everything. It is a free, volunteer-run server founded in 2017 by a group of long-time players and running on the SWGEmu project, and its own site reports over 800 active players each week, which is a good crowd for a game Sony shut down in 2011.

The draw is the original Pre-CU skill system. There are no levels and no class locks, just 34 or more professions across combat, support, crafting and the Force, and you mix them how you like. So being a dancer, a doctor or a shipwright is a real career, and the economy depends on players actually making things. Player cities, harvesters and the resource hunt make it a true sandbox.

Jedi remains the top elite profession, and you have to earn it. Unlocking it goes through a separate process built around the Village of Aurilia, which Infinity speeds up with accelerated experience, although players still call it a grind. The server keeps guides for professions and for the Jedi path, and they are worth reading. It is unofficial and has no connection to Sony or Lucasfilm. For the later version of the game, see SWG Legends.

expected.longDescription: The full modern RVGL package for Re-Volt on Windows, with the updated high-definition engine, the classic soundtrack, Dreamcast bonus content and online play.

set.longDescription:
This edition is the plain Re-Volt experience on a modern engine. Acclaim's 1999 racer put you in control of radio-controlled cars tearing through neighbourhoods, museums, supermarkets and toy shops, where everyday objects become huge obstacles, and RVGL is the open-source rewrite that makes it run natively on modern systems. This setup keeps to the original content, without the large library of community cars and tracks.

The game's joy lies in its scale and its physics. Each of its 28 or so cars has its own acceleration, top speed and weight, and all of them are light enough to flip over if you take a kerb wrong. Pickups such as bottle rockets and oil slicks add a healthy dose of chaos, so a good lead is never safe for long.

There is plenty for one player. Practice, Single Race, Time Trial and Championship modes are all here, with increasingly difficult tournaments that unlock new tracks and cars. It also shipped with a track editor, in case you feel like building your own. Choose this one for a nostalgic run through the game as you remember it, or the RVGL Online edition if you want to race the community at scheduled events. RVGL also adds split-screen play for friends on a single PC.
